opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because it sits at the heart of what we mean by a "world model."

The way I see it, the state of a system is the minimal, sufficient description of the world at a given moment that lets you predict what happens next, given some action or intervention. It's not the raw observation. A camera gives you pixels, but pixels aren't the state. The state is something more compressed and more abstract: where the objects are, what their properties are, how they relate to each other, maybe even things you can't directly see, like the mass of an object or the intention of another agent.

In classical control theory or physics, state is quite clean. If you know a particle's position and velocity, plus the forces, you can roll it forward. The real world is much messier. Observations are partial and noisy, and much of what matters is hidden. So in practice the state is always something you have to *infer*. It's a belief, a representation you construct, not something handed to you.

That's why I think representation learning and world modeling are really two sides of the same coin. If you learn a good representation, you've essentially discovered a good state space, one where the dynamics become simpler and more predictable. A bad representation keeps a lot of irrelevant detail, like the texture of every leaf, and misses the things that are causally important.

One point I find really interesting is that "state" isn't purely objective. It depends on what you care about and what you want to do. A state description that's good for a robot picking up a cup is different from one that's good for predicting the weather. So there's a task-dependent, or at least purpose-dependent, aspect to it. The hope, and maybe the big open question, is whether there's a general-purpose state representation, something like the way humans seem to carry around a common-sense model of the world that transfers across many tasks.

So in short, to me state is the compressed, predictive, and ideally actionable summary of the world. Most of the hard problems in building intelligent systems come down to learning that summary well from very high-dimensional, messy sensory data.

r001.rationale: The response calls state a minimal, sufficient description of the world for predicting what happens next, but does not say it captures all of the system’s conditions.

r002.rationale: It explicitly relates state to representation, saying that learning a good representation amounts to discovering a good state space.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually a question I've been sitting with a lot lately, because I think "state" is one of those words that gets used very loosely in our field right now, and it means different things depending on whether you're coming from reinforcement learning, from vision, or from the representation learning side.

The way I think about it: a state is the compressed summary of everything about the world that matters for what happens next. That's the key phrase for me, "what matters for what happens next." A raw video frame isn't a state. It's an observation. It has way more information than you need, and at the same time it's missing things you do need, like velocity, or what's behind the object, or what the agent was intending to do. The state is what you'd get if you threw away everything irrelevant and kept everything predictive.

And that's exactly why I find it interesting from a vision perspective. Most of my career has been about learning representations from pixels, and for a long time the implicit goal was, can this representation support recognition? Classify the image, segment the object. But that's a fairly static notion. When you start thinking about world models, or agents that act over time, the question changes. Now the representation has to carry forward. It has to be something you can roll forward in time, update when a new observation arrives, and reason about counterfactually. That's a much stronger requirement than "is this a cat."

So in my mind, a good state has a few properties. It should be sufficient, meaning that given the state, the past observations add nothing. It should be compact, because if your state is just the entire history, you haven't really understood anything. And it should be actionable, in the sense that the dynamics in state space should be simple enough that a model can learn them. A lot of the intelligence is really in the choice of what to represent, not in the dynamics model itself.

What I find humbling is that humans do this effortlessly. You walk into a room, and within a second you have a working state of that room, and you don't remember the pixels at all. Our models are still quite far from that. A lot of the current self-supervised work, including some of the things I've worked on, is really an attempt to get the representation to be more like a state and less like a feature for classification. Whether that's the right path, I honestly don't know yet. But I think it's the right question.

r001.rationale: The response defines state as a compact summary of information relevant to what happens next, but does not say it minimally describes all of the system’s conditions.

r002.rationale: It connects state to representation, describing the goal of making learned representations more like states and discussing what a representation must support.

astra-6.text:
I think of a system’s state as a snapshot of the information that matters for how it will behave next. It’s more than what you can observe on the surface; it can include internal variables or memory that influence its response.

For example, if you’re describing a moving object, knowing its position isn’t enough. You also need its velocity. Two objects can be at the same position but move very differently a moment later. In that sense, the state captures what you need to carry forward from the past to describe the system’s evolution, given new inputs.

And what counts as a state depends on the level at which you’re modeling the system. You don’t necessarily need every microscopic detail—just the information relevant to the behavior you’re trying to understand.

r001.rationale: The response describes information relevant to predicting behavior and says microscopic details may be unnecessary, but it does not characterize the state as the minimum information sufficient to describe all system conditions.

r002.rationale: It mentions that the state depends on the modeling level, but does not raise how a system’s state relates to its representation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of a system’s state as a snapshot of the information that matters for what happens next. It’s more than the output you can observe at a particular moment; it includes the internal conditions that determine how the system will respond to an input.

Take a learning system: its parameters are part of its state. During training, the optimizer’s accumulated statistics can also matter. Two systems might produce the same output right now but evolve differently because those internal states differ.

So when we talk about state, we have to specify the boundary of the system and what we want to predict. A useful state description retains enough information about the past to explain the system’s future behavior, without having to replay its entire history.

r001.rationale: The response says state retains enough information to explain future behavior, but does not characterize it as the minimum information sufficient to describe all of the system’s conditions.

r002.rationale: The response discusses state and internal information but does not raise or describe its relation to representation.
